title: Influence of Resistance Training Proximity-to-Failure on Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis
authors: Refalo MC, Helms ER, Trexler ET, Hamilton DL, Fyfe JJ
population: 15 randomised trials in healthy adults of any age and training experience that measured muscle hypertrophy: nine compared training to set failure with non-failure (seven in untrained and two in resistance-trained people) and six, all in resistance-trained people, compared velocity-loss thresholds. No strength or running outcome. Not runners.
findings: Studies were grouped into three themes by how failure was defined: momentary muscular failure against non-failure (5 studies), other definitions of set failure against non-failure (4) and different velocity-loss thresholds (6). Quality on the TESTEX scale ranged from 7 to 12 of 15 (mean 9.9); every study lost points for allocation concealment and activity monitoring.

Any definition of set failure against non-failure: a trivial advantage for failure (ES 0.19, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.37, p = 0.045). The result lost significance when the assumed pre-post correlation was below 0.73, so the authors call it uncertain. Volume load (p = 0.884) and relative load (p = 0.525) did not moderate it.

Momentary muscular failure against non-failure: no difference (ES 0.12, -0.13 to 0.37, p = 0.343). A velocity loss above 25% against 20-25%: no difference (ES 0.08, -0.16 to 0.32, p = 0.529). Within-group changes were smaller at a velocity loss under 20% (ES 0.20) than at 20-25% (0.39) and above 25% (0.42).

The authors conclude that there is no evidence that training to momentary failure is superior to non-failure training for muscle hypertrophy, that closer proximity to failure does not always give more hypertrophy, and that methods of ending a non-failure set limit what can be said about the proximity actually reached.
limitations: Hypertrophy only: no strength, running economy or injury outcome. Fifteen mostly small trials, seven of the nine failure comparisons in untrained people, and the authors say the subgroup analyses are underpowered. The proximity to failure in the non-failure arms is not measured, and one velocity-loss study found that a 40% loss ended on momentary failure in about 56% of sets. Eight studies did not describe randomisation and none concealed allocation. A comment (Fonseca 2023, 10.1007/s40279-023-01946-6) and the authors' response (10.1007/s40279-023-01947-5) are paywalled letters with no abstract and were not read. Two authors earn income as writers and practitioners in the fitness industry, as the paper declares.
implications: Hypertrophy is not the goal of the strength block, so this record is context: it finds no sign that training to failure beats stopping short, and it says the proximity actually reached by a non-failure arm is unknown. That agrees with the strength reviews of grgic-2022-failure-vs-nonfailure and vieira-2021-failure-vs-nonfailure and with the reading of `f7.heavyRir` as a target of 1-3 left.
It gives no number for how far from failure to stop and nothing for runners.

r4.note: For the statement that failure is not shown to be superior: grgic-2022-failure-vs-nonfailure and vieira-2021-failure-vs-nonfailure (different groups; the reviews share trials). Vieira found a hypertrophy advantage for failure overall that disappears with volume equated; Grgic found one for trained people (two studies). The conservative reading is no proven advantage, either way.

r5.note: Population stated: 15 trials, healthy adults, mostly untrained for the failure comparisons, hypertrophy outcomes only. Use for strength, for the heavy sets of 3-6 repetitions and for runners is extrapolated.
